title: Bonds Explained: Why Prices Fall When Rates Rise
description:
Bonds explained simply: a bond is a loan. Lend a friend $1,000 for 10 years at 4%, and you get $40 of interest (the coupon) each year and your $1,000 back at the end (maturity). If rates then rise and new bonds pay 5%, nobody will pay $1,000 for your $40 a year, so your bond's price falls to about $923: the price at which a buyer earns 5% a year, counting the $77 gain at maturity.

Our own simplified example, all numbers computed: interest paid once a year (many bonds pay twice a year), 10 years left when rates move, no fees or taxes. Holding to maturity gets you the $1,000 back only if the borrower doesn't default; selling early locks in today's price. The longer the time left, the more a bond's price moves when rates change. Not financial advice.

visual.label: your bond's price, after rates rose

scenes.say: A bond is a loan: lend a friend a thousand for ten years.
He pays forty dollars a year: the coupon, four percent.
In year ten, he repays the thousand. That's maturity.
The twist: rates rise. New bonds pay five percent.
Who pays a thousand for your forty, when new bonds pay fifty?
So its price drops to about nine hundred twenty-three, where buyers earn five percent.

visual.label: your bond's new price
visual.sub: buyer earns 5%/yr incl. $77 gain at maturity

scenes.say: Rates up, prices down. Rates down, prices up.
Hold, and if he pays, your thousand returns. Still just four percent.
Sell early, and that drop is real.
